title: Gameweek 5 Debrief: winners, blanks, and what the underlying numbers say
dek: Semenyo led Gameweek 5 with 17 points against an average of 48. Underneath the scoreline, the expected-goals numbers point at a different set of names.
body:
## The headline

**Semenyo** was the story of Gameweek 5: 17 points from 2 goals and 1 assist at home to SUN, in 90 minutes. He went into the round owned by 15.2% of managers.

:::takeaways
- **Semenyo** top-scored with 17 against SUN.
- The average manager scored **48**; the best score in the game was **126**.
- **João Pedro** (66.3% owned) returned 0 — the round's most expensive blank.
- **467,900** managers played a Wildcard.
:::

## The round in numbers

These are the figures FPL publishes about the gameweek itself rather than about any one player, and they set the bar every squad is measured against.

| Metric | Value | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Average score | **48** | What the field scored |
| Highest score | **126** | The best single squad in the game |
| Managers ranked | 10,833,606 | Squads that scored this round |
| Most captained | **Haaland** | 73.6% owned, returned 6 |
| Most selected | **Haaland** | 73.6% owned |

### Chips played

| Chip | Managers | Share of the field |
|---|---|---|
| Wildcard | **467,900** | 4.3% |
| Free Hit | **295,196** | 2.7% |
| Triple Captain | **226,208** | 2.1% |
| Bench Boost | **135,186** | 1.2% |

Wildcard was the round's most-played chip. A chip played in the same week as everybody else converts a good week into an average one relative to the field, which is the argument for holding until your own squad is ready rather than until the template says go.

The other side of the same weekend: **João Pedro** (66.3% owned) returned 0, **Wissa** (18.8% owned) returned 0, **Dubravka** (17.3% owned) returned 0, **Raya** (42.1% owned) returned 1. Points you do not score cost exactly as much as points you do, and a blank from a widely-owned player is the one everybody feels at once.
:::

## The scoreline against the underlying data

Expected goals measure the chances a player got into. Goals measure what he did with them. Over one round the gap between the two is mostly noise, but it is the right place to look for the returns that have not landed yet.

**Wissa** generated 0.84 expected goals and scored 0. That is the kind of return that tends to arrive late rather than never — provided the chances keep coming.

:::callout data
One round is one round. Everything above describes what happened in Gameweek 5; none of it is a verdict on anybody's finishing. A single game of expected-goals data has an error bar wide enough to drive a bus through. Ask again after five.
:::

## The defensive audit

7 teams kept a clean sheet in Gameweek 5: BRE, BHA, COV, CRY, EVE, LEE, LIV. Clean sheets are worth four points to a defender and a goalkeeper, which makes the defensive picture worth as much attention as the attacking one.

### Goalkeepers

| Player | Team | Price | Pts | Saves | Conceded | Owned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rushworth | COV | £4.5m | **11** | 2 | 0 | 0.8% |
| Trafford | LEE | £5.0m | **10** | 5 | 0 | 5.5% |
| Pickford | EVE | £5.5m | **8** | 4 | 0 | 9.1% |
| A.Becker | LIV | £5.5m | **8** | 2 | 0 | 3.9% |
| Kelleher | BRE | £5.0m | **6** | 2 | 0 | 6.2% |
| Verbruggen | BHA | £4.5m | **6** | 2 | 0 | 21.7% |

A goalkeeper behind a leaky defence is not automatically a bad pick: save points accumulate in exactly the weeks a clean sheet does not arrive, which is why the busiest keeper in the division is often better value than the one behind the best defence.

**MCI** scored the most goals of the round with 5. Team-level attacking output is the cleanest signal available after a single round: it takes eleven players to create a goal and one to finish it, and the finisher changes far more often than the creating does.

## The bonus point picture

Bonus is decided by the Bonus Points System, which rewards goals and assists heavily but also pays for tackles, recoveries, clean sheets and passing accuracy. Over a season it is worth roughly a point a game to the players who consistently rank in it, and it is the most overlooked component of a captaincy decision.

| Player | Team | Pos | Bonus | BPS | Pts | Owned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Brobbey** | SUN | FWD | **3** | 92 | 17 | 6.6% |
| **Buendía** | AVL | MID | **3** | 50 | 12 | 0.9% |
| **Groß** | BHA | MID | **3** | 47 | 14 | 26.8% |

| **Dasilva** | COV | DEF | **3** | 40 | 15 | 0.7% |
| **Hall** | NEW | DEF | **3** | 38 | 13 | 16.4% |

| **Trafford** | LEE | GK | **3** | 34 | 10 | 5.5% |

**Brobbey** took the maximum with 3 from a BPS score of 92. Defenders and holding midfielders who accumulate BPS through defensive actions are the ones worth identifying early, because that route to bonus is far more repeatable than the one that runs through scoring goals.

## The premium watch

A premium at £10m or more is not competing with the other forwards. He is competing with the two mid-price players you could field instead, and with the 73.6% of the field who already own the most popular of them.

| Player | Team | Price | Pts | Mins | G | A | xGI | Owned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Haaland | MCI | £15.6m | **6** | 90 | 1 | 0 | 1.11 | 73.6% |
| B.Fernandes | MUN | £12.0m | **2** | 90 | 0 | 0 | 0.45 | 38.9% |
| Palmer | CHE | £9.7m | **2** | 90 | 0 | 0 | 0.31 | 26.5% |
| Isak | LIV | £9.1m | **8** | 80 | 1 | 0 | 0.77 | 22.2% |
| Saka | ARS | £9.5m | **2** | 80 | 0 | 0 | 0.89 | 13.4% |

**Isak** led the bracket with 8. **B.Fernandes** returned 2, and at £12.0m that is the single largest hole a squad can have in a week. Not owning the most-selected premium is an active bet against 73.6% of the field — a legitimate one, but it should be deliberate.

## Enablers and budget gems

The cheapest player who actually starts is worth more than a better player who does not. An enabler's job is to cost £4.5m and play ninety minutes; everything past that is profit that funds the rest of the squad.

| Player | Team | Pos | Price | Pts | Mins | Owned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dasilva | COV | DEF | £4.0m | **15** | 90 | 0.7% |

**Dasilva** at £4.0m returned 15 points from 90 minutes, on 0.7% ownership. Enablers at that price are how squads afford two premiums without hollowing out the bench.

## The differentials who paid

Points from a player most of the field does not own are worth more than the same points from one they do. These returned at least six while owned by under 8% of managers, which is where rank is actually won.

**Brobbey** at 6.6% ownership returned 17. The managers who owned him gained ground on almost the entire field in a single afternoon — that is the whole case for carrying one or two genuine differentials rather than a squad indistinguishable from the template.

## Is Semenyo worth chasing?

The reflex after a haul is to buy it, and the reflex is usually wrong — you pay a risen price for a performance that has already happened. The question worth asking is not what he just did but what is in front of him:

:::fixtures
GW6 | LIV (A) | 4
GW7 | IPS (H) | 2
GW8 | AVL (A) | 4
GW9 | BHA (H) | 2
:::

An average difficulty of 3 across his next four. That is an ordinary run — not a reason to buy and not a reason to avoid, which usually means the transfer is better spent elsewhere.

## The early transfer radar

Four calls off the back of this round, with the reasoning attached so you can disagree with the reasoning rather than the conclusion.

:::actions
buy | Brobbey (SUN, £5.7m) | 2.82 expected involvements in 90 minutes and still only 6.6% owned.
buy | Anthony (BRE, £5.9m) | 0.98 expected involvements in 80 minutes and still only 0.1% owned.
hold | Calvert-Lewin (£6.0m) | 2 points reads badly, but 0.52 expected involvements says the process was fine. Selling here sells the scoreline, not the player.
sell | João Pedro (£7.8m) | Knee injury - 75% chance of playing
:::
